implementation_notes: The document is a .proto message and protoc generates a class per message with typed accessors (set_/mutable_/clear_, add_/size_ helpers for repeated fields) plus SerializeToString/ParseFromString, SerializeToOstream/ParseFromIstream and PackFrom/UnpackTo for Any. Field numbers rather than names form the contract, so additive changes stay compatible in both directions and unknown fields survive a round trip; the .proto file is the versioned artifact shared with the other languages. Current protobuf C++ requires a C++17 compiler, which is the floor of this variant; it is the default because schema-first documents scale to several languages and consumers.
pitfalls: Field numbers, wire types and presence rules are the compatibility contract - renaming a field is safe, renumbering or reusing a tag is not.
Accessor results returned by const reference (name(), lines(i)) are invalidated by any subsequent non-const call on the message; never cache them across mutation.
The codegen toolchain is part of the build: a stale generated header against a newer runtime fails at link time or at runtime.

variants.name: nlohmann::json dynamic document tree
variants.implementation_notes: When the document is JSON and its shape is decided at runtime, the single-header nlohmann::json library supplies the document type itself: basic_json is default-constructible to null, buildable from literals, navigable with operator[] and iterators, and convertible to the other formats it speaks (from_cbor/from_msgpack and friends). Wire names come from the object keys rather than an IDL, NLOHMANN_JSON_SERIALIZE_ENUM maps enums to strings, and the receiver inspects keys and types to decide what to do. Choose it when no schema registry exists and the peer only speaks JSON; the absence of a compiled contract is the trade.
pitfalls: parse() throws on malformed input and operator[] on a const tree throws out_of_range for a missing key; both must be handled or one bad document crashes the consumer.
The document schema lives only in code, so producer and consumer drift silently until a field turns out to be missing at runtime.
The tree owns a copy of every string, so large documents pay for two representations (wire buffer plus tree).

variants.name: FlatBuffers zero-copy documents
variants.idiom_name: FlatBufferBuilder + generated accessors on the wire buffer
variants.implementation_notes: FlatBuffers compiles a .fbs schema into accessors that read fields directly out of the serialized buffer, so the receiver never parses: FlatBufferBuilder builds the document from native types, GetRoot<T>() returns a typed view and flatbuffers::Verifier validates an untrusted buffer before it is dereferenced. That removes the parse step and the document-wide allocation, which is why it wins where volume and latency dominate (telemetry, game-style payloads); the price is a rigid schema-evolution discipline plus a build-time code generator.
pitfalls: An unverified buffer is a security hole: always run the Verifier before touching a document that arrived from outside.
The buffer must outlive every accessor view - returning a table whose storage died with a local DetachedBuffer is a use-after-free.
Schema evolution has to be additive and defaulted; reordering or removing fields corrupts readers compiled against the old schema.
